cases.community: The completion report of 25 April 2013 records what it calls a serious case of non-compliance with the project's resettlement plan at the wastewater treatment plant. In its words, it "was brought to public attention when a deeply frustrated person attempted suicide in 2006 in a prominent public location." The report gives three causes. The urban master plan for the area where the plant was to be built was changed after the Bank's Board approved the project; the Bank was not told the plant boundary had moved, the resettlement plan was not updated, and the newly affected people were not consulted. Under the original plan the man was not expected to be affected at all; after the boundary was revised his house, and those of several neighbours, fell inside the project area. A dispute then began between him, his neighbours and the local government, and the report says the project's grievance system "did not work effectively and the dispute escalated quickly." The external monitoring team knew of the dispute before it escalated and did not report it to the government or the Bank. The report says central, provincial and municipal governments and the Bank intervened, a resettlement consultant was hired, a relocation implementation plan was drawn up and the breaches were resolved to the Bank's satisfaction; resettlement "remained demanding and continued to cause construction delays, but no further non-compliance occurred." It lists general reasons for the non-compliance: compensation requirements poorly estimated, costs significantly underestimated, the complaints mechanism insufficient, implementation capacity over-estimated, design changes not fed back into the revised plan, counterpart funds that could not be assured, and project units without enough experience. Two other sections record trouble. In Zhaoshan, resettlement stagnated in 2005 and was severely delayed because the compensation estimate rose from RMB 42.98 million to RMB 82.38 million and the money could not be raised; the report says efforts "made little difference" and the capital bottleneck was not resolved. In Zhuzhou's Tianyuan District the report says there were not enough resettlement houses, supply fell short of demand, and for some households the transitional period ran to more than two years, which it says caused disputes and complaints. Annex 8 gives the resettlement in each section as planned against actual. Changsha: 744 households and 3,051 people resettled, against 502 households and 1,902 people in the plan. Xiangtan urban area: 331 households and 810 people affected by house demolition, against 341 and 1,107 planned. Zhaoshan: 12 households and 65 people, against 192 and 803 planned. Zhuzhou: 714 households and 1,963 people, against 591 and 1,620 planned. Zhuzhou Leidashi: 54 households and 175 people, against 257 and 901 planned. Changshanyuan wastewater treatment plant: 26 households and 110 people relocated, against 6 and 20 planned. Resettlement spending in the Changsha section rose from RMB 122.38 million at appraisal to RMB 590.09 million, close to five times the plan; in Xiangtan from RMB 77.74 million to RMB 241.68 million. 112 vulnerable households in the Changsha section and seven at the wastewater plant received special subsidies, the latter RMB 5,000 each. Annex 8 names one community. It records that in June 2009 villagers of Huanghe Village put their dissatisfaction with the resettlement arrangement to the World Bank, that a Bank team visited the village with the provincial project office, and that a solution was reached through consultation. On incomes, the annex reports a fall and then a recovery in the Changsha section: follow-up surveys in 2007, 2008 and 2009 found that in 2007 per capita net income was 21.2 per cent below the level before resettlement, which the report attributes to the land acquisition and resettlement then under way, to "the failures in implementing the production resettlement measures and rehabilitating production of resettled people", and to resettled people spending their time building new houses rather than on production. It says income then grew in 2008 and 2009. For the other sections it reports per capita net income after resettlement up 29.3 per cent in Xiangtan, 58.8 per cent in Zhaoshan, 60.5 per cent in Zhuzhou and 74.3 per cent at Leidashi, and surveyed households satisfied or basically satisfied. At the wastewater plant the report says that before May 2007 the public participation and complaint mechanism was not working satisfactorily, and that it was improved after May 2007. At Leidashi the works could not start in 2008 because all residents of Leidashi town had to be moved and funds were short, so the dike design was changed to a flood control wall to reduce the land needed.
cases.killed_note: The completion report records an attempted suicide in 2006 by a man whose house was brought inside the wastewater treatment plant site after the plan was revised. It does not say he died, and no death is counted here.
cases.outcome: The resettlement was completed and the breach was closed out. The completion report of 25 April 2013 rates the project outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Moderate. Within Bank performance it rates quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory and quality of supervision Satisfactory. It records that the project was a potential problem project and a problem project at some point during implementation. The World Bank's document set for this project lists 31 documents and contains no Implementation Completion Report Review, and a search of the Bank's document service for an Independent Evaluation Group review of this project returns none, so no second rating is given here. Resettlement completion reports for the sections were submitted in March 2013.
cases.displaced_label: people whose houses were demolished or who were resettled, in 1,881 households, added across the six per-section tables in Annex 8 of the World Bank completion report
cases.displaced_note: The figure is the sum of the actual-amount rows for people affected by house demolition or resettled in each of the six sections in Annex 8 of the World Bank's completion report: Changsha 3,051 people in 744 households, Xiangtan urban area 810 in 331, Zhaoshan 65 in 12, Zhuzhou 1,963 in 714, Zhuzhou Leidashi 175 in 54, and the Changshanyuan wastewater treatment plant 110 in 26. The report labels these rows differently from section to section - "number of resettled people" in Changsha, "affected by household demolition" in four sections, "number of people relocated" at the wastewater plant - and it prints no project-wide total. The 744 households and 3,051 people in the Changsha section are the rows the report labels "number of resettled households" and "number of resettled people"; at the wastewater plant the rows are labelled "number of people relocated" and "number of households relocated". ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 11,214 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents cited here do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Chongqing Small Cities Infrastructure Improvement Project, P081161. Loan 4794-CHA of US$180 million, approved 21 June 2005, closed 30 June 2012 on the original closing date. US$175.09 million was disbursed. The project was restructured on 25 February 2009 and 7 June 2010. Total project cost was US$352.06 million against US$264.5 million estimated at appraisal.

cases.conditions: The loan triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement and safety of dams. Resettlement action plans were prepared. At appraisal it was estimated that about 13,700 people would be affected by land acquisition and house demolition and that 270 hectares would be acquired. Chongqing Technology and Business University was appointed as the external independent monitoring agent for the social safeguards.
cases.community: Two documents of the Bank record this resettlement, and the completion report they draw on is not in the Bank's public document set. The Independent Evaluation Group, reviewing that report on 3 September 2013, records two failures reported by the project's external monitoring agent. First, the internal monitoring of resettlement by the project implementation units was inadequate. Second, land compensation was delayed and housing compensation rates were lower than those agreed in the resettlement action plan, "particularly for the Tongnan road construction activities"; the review says the compensation problems in Tongnan were later corrected. It also records that at project closing a resettlement action involving 48 households, roughly 200 people, in Qianjiang County remained unfinished, and adds: "As confirmed by the TTL, this resettlement activity as of today is still not resolved" - that is, more than a year after the loan closed on 30 June 2012. On scale, the review reports from Annex 7 of the completion report that 11,663 people were actually affected, 275.78 hectares were permanently acquired and 108,770.36 square metres of houses were demolished. The Group recommended the project for further assessment, giving the unfinished Qianjiang resettlement as its first reason, and that assessment was carried out. Its Project Performance Assessment Report of 23 June 2014, written after a field mission, gives the Qianjiang figures. A new 12.8 km road linking two towns with a combined population of 80,000 "required the demolition of 175 houses to secure the right of way". Of the residents, "127 households were resettled quickly, while 48 households did not accept a proposed relocation site." The 48 asked to be resettled near the project road, which the local authority agreed to, and asked the local government both to provide all infrastructure at the site, which the report calls a normal request, and to build foundations able to carry high-rise buildings, which it calls not a normal request; the county government paid for this at an extra cost of more than US$1 million. The mission saw heavy-duty piles being driven at the site, and records that displaced households living in temporary housing nearby said they looked forward to building their new development, moving in and renting out. The assessment report says the project "was generally in compliance with Bank safeguards", that involuntary resettlement was invoked ten times, and that apart from Qianjiang the project involved "nine other cases of resettlement affecting 14,158 people at a total cost of about US$36 million", with no case of non-compliance reported in those nine. On the Tongnan compensation rates the two documents do not agree, and both are printed here: the review of September 2013 records housing compensation rates lower than those agreed in the plan, later corrected; the assessment report of June 2014 says that in all ten cases the planning of the resettlement and the provision of compensation "were reportedly compliant" with the Bank's policy. Separately, the number of public toilets financed was cut from 235 to 153 because local residents objected to where they were to be put and because of what the review calls persistent land acquisition and resettlement problems. No village or neighbourhood is named in either document.
cases.outcome: The project closed with the Qianjiang resettlement unfinished, still unresolved in September 2013 on the Bank evaluators' account, and with piling under way at the replacement site when the evaluators visited in 2014. The completion report rated the project outcome Satisfactory, risk to the development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group downgraded three of those: outcome to Moderately Satisfactory, because the economic rates of return of some project activities were lower at completion and some were below the threshold; risk to the development outcome to Significant, citing insufficient funds for maintenance and the flood protection standards used; and borrower performance to Moderately Satisfactory, citing still "some pending issues to be addressed at project completion,e.g., resettlement activity in Qianjiang county" together with procurement management. It rated the quality of the completion report Satisfactory and said the report was open and candid about what had not worked.
cases.displaced_label: households whose houses were demolished for the Qianjiang road, 127 of them resettled quickly and 48 refusing the site offered; the completion report counts 11,663 people affected across the whole project and 108,770.36 square metres of housing demolished
cases.displaced_note: The only count of households displaced that the Bank's documents give is for Qianjiang. The Independent Evaluation Group's assessment report of 23 June 2014 says the road there required the demolition of 175 houses, that 127 households were resettled quickly and that 48 households did not accept the relocation site proposed. The 48 are the households the Group's earlier review of 3 September 2013 recorded as an unfinished resettlement at closing, roughly 200 people; they are part of the Qianjiang total, not the scale of the project's resettlement. For the project as a whole the review reports from Annex 7 of the completion report that 11,663 people were affected by land acquisition and house demolition, against about 13,700 estimated at appraisal, and that 108,770.36 square metres of houses were demolished; "affected" is the word the document uses and it is not a count of people relocated. The assessment report adds that nine further cases of resettlement, outside Qianjiang, affected 14,158 people at a cost of about US$36 million, again as people affected. The completion report itself is not in the World Bank's public document set: the Bank's document service lists 23 documents for this project, including the Group's review, the Group's assessment report, the appraisal document, two resettlement plans and implementation status reports, but no completion report. The completion report's figures given here are therefore as the Group quotes them, with the report's page and annex numbers. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 13,744 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. That is close to, but not the same as, the appraisal estimate of about 13,700 affected people. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents cited here do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

cases.title: Sichuan Urban Development: 3,262 households moved in four cities
cases.place: Mianyang, Suining, Panzhihua and Yibin municipalities, Sichuan, China
cases.point: Approximate. The coordinates sit on the city of Mianyang, which had the largest recorded resettlement of the four. The project built roads, bridges and pipelines in Mianyang, Suining, Panzhihua and Yibin, and each municipality ran its own resettlement.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Sichuan Urban Development Project, P083322. Loan IBRD-48380, also written 4838-CHA, of US$180.00 million, approved 7 September 2006, signed 27 October 2006, effective 5 January 2007, restructured 18 August 2011, closed 31 December 2013 on the original closing date. All US$180.00 million was disbursed. The borrower was the People's Republic of China.

cases.conditions: The loan triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement and was environmental category A. Each of the four municipalities prepared its own resettlement action plan; the plans were disclosed in English and Chinese in October 2005. An indigenous peoples plan was also prepared, in May 2005. Because the resettlement was large the project was put on the Bank's corporate risk list and reviewed by the Bank's Resettlement Committee, which endorsed its approach at a meeting in April 2006. An expert team from Southwest China Communication University monitored the plans twice a year in each municipality and produced nine monitoring reports, then a resettlement completion report for each municipality.
cases.community: The completion report of 19 June 2014 gives the resettlement as carried out. Across the four cities 4,591.40 mu of land was acquired and 276,515.18 square metres of housing demolished, 239,798.39 square metres of it in rural areas and 36,716.79 in urban. It states that "about 10,788 people in 3,262 households were affected by the resettlement (either by land acquisition, house demolition, or both)", and that more than 3,000 further people were indirectly affected by the relocation of enterprises. Elsewhere in the same report the figure is written as households that were relocated, in a passage about the conversion of rural to urban household registration: "The project contributed to addressing this inequity for the 3,262 households that were relocated." Its table breaks the impact down. Land acquisition affected 7,177 people in 2,411 households - 172 people in 42 households in Panzhihua, 2,899 in 938 in Suining, 3,908 in 1,374 in Mianyang, 198 in 57 in Yibin. Rural house demolition affected 5,562 people in 1,903 households, urban house demolition 2,157 people in 716 households. A footnote says that in Mianyang and Suining, where the works were in economic development zones, people affected by house demolition were already counted among those affected by land acquisition. Enterprise, shop and institutional relocation affected 3,496 people in 289 units. Total resettlement cost was RMB 663.91 million. On timing, Panzhihua and Suining ran their plans from February 2008 to the end of 2012, Yibin from March 2007 to June 2012 and Mianyang from December 2007 to June 2013; the report says that although there were delays, resettlement was wholly completed when the project closed. The Wenchuan earthquake of 12 May 2008, near Mianyang, interrupted all local processes. The report says compensation rates were raised by a large margin, that resettled people could choose between three forms of housing, that most moved into officially built resettlement housing while keeping the property rights of their original houses, and that they received larger spaces than before. The same section records that one road in Suining was affected by the refusal of two households to vacate the land, which forced a redesign and narrowing of the road, prevented completion of the sidewalks, posed safety hazards and voided their full use as designed. It also says there were "a few relatively isolated cases where the lack of agreement on compensation caused implementation delays" and that otherwise there was no significant adverse impact on affected people. Satisfaction surveys are reported at 75 per cent in one Mianyang area and 60 per cent satisfied with 40 per cent basically satisfied in two others, and 63.2 per cent in Suining. The results framework counts resettlement in two streams: households resettled because of civil works, and households resettled because of land sales in the development zones. In Mianyang's Pioneer Park area the actuals are 110 households for civil works and 3,140 for land sale; in the Southern Economic Development Area 1,016 for civil works and 1,654 for land sale; in Suining's Xining area 642 for civil works and 938 for land sale. On risk, the report says the appraisal document judged most risks moderate "with just two deemed substantial (delay in land sales and inadequate compensation levels)", that no aggregate rating was assigned, and that the overall risk profile "should have been at least “substantial” if not “high”, especially considering the reputational risks and controversy surrounding the land valuation and resettlement". No village or neighbourhood is named in the report.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant. The completion report of 19 June 2014 rates the project outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Substantial; within Bank performance it rates quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory. It records that the project was a potential problem project and a problem project at some point in implementation. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 23 February 2015 keeps outcome at Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance at Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance at Satisfactory, and records no reason for disagreement; its table prints the risk rating, in both its own column and the column for the completion report, as Significant, where the completion report's own data sheet prints Substantial. Both documents report the same named shortfall in the resettlement: on one road in Suining two households refused to accept the established compensation norms, the road was redesigned and narrowed, its footways were not completed, and this posed safety hazards and voided the full use of the road as designed. The Group prints it as a lesson and says the implementing agency should have settled with the residents before construction went ahead, or changed the design. It also records that resettlement costs for Route A in Yibin were 61 per cent higher than the appraisal estimate, and that a tracer study designed to follow the conversion of rural residents to urban status was never carried out and the question never got substantive attention in supervision missions, so the Bank, in its words, missed an opportunity to look at land value and the benefits for the rural population whose land was converted.

lenders.role: Jiangxi Wuxikou Integrated Flood Management Project, P128867. Loan IBRD-82370 of US$100,000,000, approved 20 March 2013, effective 19 July 2013, mid-term review 21 April 2016, reallocated between disbursement categories 25 April 2019 and extended on 26 June 2019. The closing date moved from 30 June 2019 to 30 June 2020. All US$100,000,000 was disbursed. The borrower and recipient put in US$486,930,000 against US$413,720,000 planned, for a total project cost of US$586,930,000 against US$513,720,000 at appraisal.

cases.conditions: The loan triggered the Bank's policy on involuntary resettlement, because of the land acquisition and population relocation the reservoir and dam required, and its policy on safety of dams. A resettlement action plan was prepared and later updated with the Bank's approval. Resettlement was a component of the project in its own right. A group of sociologists from Hohai University in Nanjing acted as the external monitoring agency and also ran the resettlement satisfaction survey. A dam safety panel of three independent specialists was established by the project management office. Compensation for displaced farmers was set by the plan as a homestead plot for building a replacement house for physically displaced households and 0.04 hectares of farmland for each economically displaced person, and the government runs a 20-year post-resettlement support programme.
cases.community: The completion report of 26 January 2021 counts the resettlement. By project closure 31,940 mu, about 9.6 square kilometres, of land had been acquired. 10,469 people in 2,331 households were physically displaced; of those, 9,402 were permanently relocated to one of 29 resettlement sites and 1,067 moved into their own houses in urban areas. A footnote says the 9,402 includes 882 people from administrative and institutional organisations and enterprises who moved to the new Chitan downtown area. A further 5,339 people were economically displaced only, losing livelihoods or businesses. The report says the physically displaced households normally lost land and other means of livelihood including business. In all, it says, 15,808 people were adversely affected and were compensated with a mix of cash and land. Chitan town, which the report calls the only town relocated, was rebuilt with school, hospital and market. Demolished roads and railway were restored. The number of physically displaced people rose from 10,200 anticipated at appraisal to 10,469; the project's own results indicator, "No. of people relocated with proper compensation and livelihood restoration", had a target of 10,104 and is recorded at 10,469 at completion, dated 20 June 2020. The borrower's section of the report counts the same 10,469 differently: 9,587 resettled people from 2,332 local households plus 882 resettled people from administrative and institutional organisations and enterprises, and of the 9,587 it says 7,872 were resettled together at sites, 648 moved for scattered resettlement and 1,067 took cash compensation. A linked project, the Wuxikou city dike system in Jingdezhen, affected 340 rural households with 1,536 farmers through land acquisition and relocated a further 210 rural households with 927 farmers and 526 urban households with 2,048 residents; the report says it applied the same standards and was monitored by the same agency. The report records one source of delay in the resettlement component: by the original closing date of 30 June 2019 the resettled people's demands had changed from the original plan because their circumstances had changed, and additional consultations on the replacement housing were held, the plan was updated and approved by the Bank, and the closing date was extended. Two prolonged rainy seasons, in 2016 and 2018, interrupted housing construction, and affected people asked to build their own new homes so as to earn income from the work. The report says compensation was paid on time and in full as planned, incomes were restored, 97.3 per cent of physically displaced households moved into permanent housing, resettled people's income per head reached RMB 16,678 in 2019 against a Fuliang County average of RMB 16,521 in 2018, and a resettlement association committee was set up at each of the 29 village resettlement sites. The Hohai University survey reports 99.56 per cent of resettled people satisfied with their land and housing, 95.58 per cent with the impact compensation and 97.79 per cent with the resettlement arrangements, and no grievances.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant. A resettlement completion report reviewed the whole process and, the completion report says, found it carried out in compliance with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy and with Chinese law; the project's overall social safeguards performance is rated Satisfactory. The completion report of 26 January 2021 rates the project outcome Highly Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality High. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 April 2021 gives the same three ratings and records no reason for disagreement, and rates the quality of the completion report Substantial. The Group repeats the figures and the compliance finding from the completion report and adds no finding of its own about the resettlement. The dam is the fourth on the Changjiang River.
cases.displaced_label: people physically displaced, in 2,331 households, of whom 9,402 moved to one of 29 resettlement sites and 1,067 into their own urban houses; a further 5,339 people were economically displaced only (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: The World Bank's completion report distinguishes the two kinds of displacement. 10,469 people in 2,331 households were physically displaced. 5,339 more people were economically displaced only, which the report defines here as permanent loss of livelihoods or businesses. It puts the total adversely affected at 15,808 people. The physically displaced figure rose from 10,200 anticipated at appraisal, against a results-framework target of 10,104. The borrower's section of the same report splits the 10,469 as 9,587 people from 2,332 local households and 882 people from organisations and enterprises, where the Bank's section gives 2,331 households. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 10,957 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table; the documents cited here contain no figure of 10,957 and do not explain the gap. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents cited here do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

lenders.role: Da Nang Sustainable City Development Project, P123384. Credit IDA-52330 of US$202,500,000, approved 26 April 2013, effective 29 July 2013, plus additional financing IDA-60320 of US$72,520,000 approved 31 May 2017. Revised to US$127,381,118 and US$24,500,471 after a cancellation on 4 June 2021; US$117,175,564 and US$24,500,471 were disbursed. The closing date moved from 30 June 2019 to 30 June 2021, and the government undertook to keep applying the Bank's safeguards until the remaining activities finished in December 2022. The borrower was the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam and the implementing agency the Danang PIIPs project management unit. Total project cost was US$248,586,035 against US$358,320,000 at appraisal, with the borrower putting in US$106,910,000.

cases.conditions: The loan triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement and was environmental category B. A resettlement policy framework and six resettlement action plans were prepared and disclosed between October 2012 and June 2021, covering the project as a whole, the Nguyen Tat Thanh road and My Da Tay resettlement site, the Hoa Phuoc-Hoa Khuong road, additional items added in 2016, the DH2 road and items added in 2020. Compensation was based on replacement cost surveys by an independent appraiser, and site-specific plans set out entitlement matrices. A grievance mechanism was set up at the start of the project.
cases.community: The completion report of 20 January 2022 says the project acquired 143.72 hectares of land, 71.75 of it agricultural, and affected 4,730 project affected people at closing, almost double the 2,855 estimated at appraisal, because of works added under the additional financing. Of those, 1,076 were relocated and 4,566 were compensated under government rules. The difference is a shortfall the report records plainly: "Despite these efforts, 164 cases were pending at project closing and the Post-Closure Action Plan included actions to resolve them." It says that between July and December 2021, after the loan closed, a further 94 households received compensation and agreed to transfer their land, and that the compensation council was still in discussion with the remaining households when the report was written. The project also relocated 1,200 graves and one pagoda; the Independent Evaluation Group says that process followed the resettlement plans and that no other cultural site was found during excavation. The Group sets out why the resettlement went slowly. New legislation in 2013 moved land acquisition and compensation to district authorities, and cities set up land fund development centres to collect data on who was eligible. The project management unit's early handling of beneficiary data produced multiple records for the same affected people, with incomplete information on which to base compensation, so the unit, the district compensation, assistance and resettlement board and local authorities had to spend time reconciling data and documenting people. Differences between Bank guidelines and local law took time to reconcile. Compensation negotiations with affected households took time. The 2017 additional financing changed the design and scope and added land acquisition and resettlement. The project took over the unfinished works of the earlier Da Nang Priority Infrastructure Investment Project, credit IDA-44020, as its Component 5, "Transferred Activities from Da Nang Priority Infrastructure Investment Project", at an original cost of US$36.8 million and an actual cost of US$26.94 million: the southern road link to the Hoa Phuoc-Hoa Khuong road, the Hoa Xuan wastewater treatment plant, the upgrading of the Son Tra plant, the Phu Loc bridge and the Phu Loc river embankment, with the construction supervision and safeguards monitoring that went with them. The earlier project's completion report says its own resettlement was completed satisfactorily "except for those acquisitions and resettlements which were transferred" to this one. The Group adds that the earlier project had already shown how complex negotiating with affected people was, and that this project's design "appeared to have underestimated the scale of land acquisition and the subsequent resettlement and rehabilitation needs". A survey found 83 per cent of households satisfied with the compensation price. One resettlement area, Hoa Lien, was built under the project. No individual household or community is named.
cases.outcome: The project closed with 164 compensation cases unresolved and a post-closure plan to deal with them. The completion report of 20 January 2022 rates the project outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 June 2022 keeps outcome and Bank performance at Moderately Satisfactory and downgrades monitoring and evaluation quality to Modest, giving as its reason weaknesses in the outcome indicators and that the monitoring data was not used to inform the additional financing. It rates the quality of the completion report Substantial. The Group also records that after 2019 resettlement and relocation data were among the things that led to targets and activities being revised and the closing date extended. On a separate matter, the State Audit of Vietnam, covering the period from project signing to 30 June 2019, found that VND 1,905 billion, which the completion report converts as US$82,382, had been paid to several contractors and consultants for ineligible expenditure and that VND 3,958 billion, converted as US$173,034, had been overpaid to a contractor; the Bank asked the government to refund US$569,858.39 and the report says this was paid in full in October 2021.

cases.community: The completion report of 22 December 2022 says that at closing the project had affected 5,367 households, of which 1,006 were relocated. It then records a breach. "Further, non-compliance with OP/BP 4.12 was noted by the World Bank in 2015 and 2020 in Phu Ly City, which was subsequently resolved." Its footnote 36 gives the three grounds: "(i) the compensation amount paid by PMU for acquisition of illegal structures did not match the replacement cost; (ii) the PMU did not provide the needed technical assistance to vulnerable households as required; and (iii) the compensation plan had not been prepared by PMU and submitted prior to the commencement of certain civil works." The report also says the project ran into delays in organising compensation payments and land acquisition because counterpart funds came late and because several households disagreed with the level of compensation offered, and that complaints through the grievance mechanism were mainly about the timeliness and the adequacy of compensation payments, all of which it says were resolved by closing. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 6 June 2023 repeats the three grounds of the breach and adds that "some houses were damaged by construction activities due to works’ terrain and geological conditions that led to some disagreements with affected households on compensation packages", that unclear land ownership required lengthy verification, that some affected households were not cooperative, and that several residents demanded what it calls excessive compensation. It adds that lengthy coordination between departments and slow disbursement of compensation to affected people pushed out land acquisition. Both documents say land acquisition, compensation and resettlement in Lao Cai city and Vinh city followed the plans and that third-party monitoring found overall high satisfaction. Graves in Vinh city were relocated as required. The ethnic minority development plan in Lao Cai was carried out adequately, with delays in 2021 because of COVID-19 restrictions on meetings. No individual household or community is named.
cases.outcome: The breach in Phu Ly was recorded and, the Bank says, resolved. The completion report of 22 December 2022 rates the project outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial, and says the project complied with the social safeguards policies "with some non-compliance activities promptly resolved as required". The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 6 June 2023 gives the same three ratings, records no reason for disagreement, and rates the quality of the completion report Substantial. The Group reports that slow release of funds from central government contributed to a significant delay in site access for early road contracts and in finishing the drainage works at the Vinh city citadel, and that slow initial progress in Vinh city came from delays in land acquisition, site clearance and resettlement, and from moving utilities, especially high voltage cables, which added costs. The closing date for Vinh city was extended to 31 December 2018 so that it could meet its targets. Audit reports raised internal control issues including projects behind schedule because of site clearance delay.

cases.community: The completion report of 2 June 2014 counts the resettlement in one paragraph. During the original credit period 265 hectares of land, primarily agricultural, were permanently acquired. "This affected 4,168 households, of which 989 households had to resettle, and 165 had their businesses and/ or more than 20 percent of their agricultural land affected." Annex 4 of the same report gives the same total of 4,168, but in a column headed "Affected people" and, on the line beneath, "(No. of persons)". The annex breaks it down by province against plan, the planned total being 3,644: Thanh Hoa 404 against 386 planned, Nghe An 282 against 253, Ha Tinh 3 against 2, Quang Binh 49 against 33, Quang Tri 1,313 against 1,223, Thua Thien Hue 8 against 8, Quang Nam 126 against 124, Quang Ngai 12 against 12, Ben Tre 755 against 390, Dong Thap 1,194 against 750, the Mekong Delta early warning system 9 against 296, and drainage along the Hanoi-Ho Chi Minh City railway 13 against 167. Resettlement cost US$8,223,565.04 against US$7,428,459.50 planned, with the largest overruns in Ben Tre and Dong Thap. The report says compensation payment, financial and livelihood restoration support and resettlement work were provided in accordance with the resettlement policy framework, that land acquisition and resettlement were carried out in full compliance with that framework, that complaints were addressed well before project closure, that affected households, particularly those severely affected, restored their livelihoods to pre-project levels, and that no ethnic minority households were adversely affected. Under the additional financing, which concentrated on post-disaster reconstruction, most works stayed inside existing land and the report says the need for land acquisition was very small, with occasional minor land donation for road rehabilitation. On the Bank's side, the report rates government performance Moderately Satisfactory and lists among the shortcomings behind that rating the "slow flow of counterpart funds for resettlement compensation". No village or commune is named.
cases.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as compliant, and the Bank's own evaluators say the record does not show it. The completion report of 2 June 2014 rates the project outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to the development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 8 December 2014 keeps the outcome at Moderately Satisfactory. On the environmental side the Group writes that according to the completion report there were no complaints from local communities and environmental safeguard policies were fully complied with, and then: "However, the ICR does not provide concrete evidence to support this claim, nor does it indicate whether a grievance mechanism was formally establish to register any such complaints." On the social side it sets out the completion report's statements that resettlement was in full compliance, that complaints were addressed well before closure, that affected households restored their livelihoods and that no ethnic minorities were harmed, and then: "However, again no concrete evidence is provided to back up these affirmations." The Group also records that post-reviews of procurement found several instances of procedural deviations and non-compliance, and that procurement delays on the Mekong Delta early warning system were largely responsible for the repeated extensions of the closing date.

The same total of 4,168 appears in the report's resettlement annex under the heading "Affected people (No. of persons)", so the report labels the same number as households in one place and as persons in another; both labels are printed here and neither is preferred. The annex gives no breakdown of the 989. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 11,643 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. No figure of 11,643 appears in the documents cited here, and they do not explain the gap. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts". Its data stops at 31 December 2014. The documents cited here do not explain how ICIJ arrived at its figure.

cases.whole: The project was to reduce the vulnerability of people in hazard-prone provinces to flood, storm and other natural hazards, make post-disaster recovery more efficient, and strengthen disaster risk management institutions. It financed infrastructure works, community-based risk management, disaster mitigation investment plans in 12 provinces and, under the additional financing, 165 post-disaster reconstruction and upgrading works on schools, health stations and other buildings for US$18.9 million. The completion report says the project was expected to benefit people living in 12 hazard-prone provinces, and elsewhere 15. Procurement and financial management were both rated only Moderately Satisfactory. The disbursed amount, SDR 104.54 million, was well above the original SDR 59 million commitment after the additional financing.

add.community_add: The earlier credit paid for a southern ring road, a southern link road, drainage and sanitation works and upgrading in 13 low income areas. Its completion report of 19 December 2013 says the project acquired around 189.1 hectares of land and affected 3,518 households, of which 1,670 lost agricultural land. On how many were resettled the two Bank documents give different numbers. The completion report says, in its safeguards section and again in the borrower's section, that of the 3,518 households 936 "were only partially affected and had to be resettled", and that the number of resettled households rose by 12 per cent against the 711 originally planned. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 23 October 2014 repeats the 936 in its own safeguards section and, in its list of the project's outputs, states that "796 households were resettled, compared to 711 originally planned". Both figures are printed here and neither document reconciles them. The completion report gives two reasons for the increase over plan: some households split their plots, two families living on one plot dividing it in two, and some households moved voluntarily to better resettlement areas closer to the Southern Link Road route. Three resettlement areas were built on 18.3 hectares in total, at Thanh Khe Tay, Hoa Minh and Hoa Quy. The Bank's section of the report says the project provided 613 lots and 198 apartments for relocated households and a school with 20 rooms for children of affected households; the borrower's section gives 1,098 lots and 110 apartments at the sites, of which 287 lots and 56 apartments were funded by this project and 811 lots and 54 apartments by the city. The report says most compensation was completed as planned, that compensation and resettlement for the southern ring road was finished by June 2013 except for the activities transferred to the later project, that all relocated households were allocated land plots at a resettlement site, that Da Nang used sites inside people's own neighbourhoods to meet their wish to stay nearby, and that the grievance system worked well. The independent resettlement monitoring consultant is quoted in the Group's review as certifying that "almost all Project affected people have been able to restore their lost assets and livelihoods." The physical cultural resources policy was triggered by the relocation of some graves and by two temples and four houses of worship in the project area; the report says consultation at appraisal found the affected people willing to relocate if compensated and given alternative sites, and that there were no adverse impacts at closure. Delays in negotiating relocation, land acquisition and resettlement are recorded in both documents as holding up construction. No individual household or community is named.
add.outcome_add: The earlier credit's completion report of 19 December 2013 rates its outcome Moderately Satisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 23 October 2014 keeps that rating. The Group records that works worth an estimated US$16.6 million, 25 per cent of the appraisal estimate, were moved to the later project, records shortcomings in the handling of land acquisition and relocation that delayed construction, and prints among the project's lessons that "relocation and resettlement should be minimized".
add.displaced_note_add: For the earlier credit the Bank's documents give two counts of households resettled. Its completion report says 936 of 3,518 affected households had to be resettled and that the number rose 12 per cent against the 711 planned. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says 936 in its safeguards section and 796 in its list of outputs. 1,670 households lost agricultural land. ICIJ puts displacement for the earlier project at 13,788 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table; no figure of 13,788 appears in these documents and they do not explain the gap.

dropped.candidate: China Anhui Highway Rehabilitation and Improvement Project (P099112)
dropped.reason: No document of this project counts anyone relocated. The completion report of 12 December 2012 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 3 June 2013 were both read in full, and the Bank's document service lists 24 documents for the project, including six volumes of resettlement planning, the appraisal document and two implementation status reports. The completion report's resettlement passage, in both the Bank's section and the borrower's, gives only areas: 2,510.09 mu of land acquisition and 31,194 square metres of house demolition, with no count of people or households anywhere in it. The counts the draft rested on are in the Group's review, which states that "the project team provided additional information on the number of people affected by the resettlement, which were 2,550 households with 9,496 persons" and that "the team confirmed that all 412 households affected by house demolition built new houses with adequate facilities." Those figures are the Bank's own project staff speaking to the Bank's evaluators during the review; no document of the project records them, and the one document that should, the completion report, does not. Under the forward rule as refined, that is not a document that counts households relocated, and the project fails the rule's second limb outright: no death, injury, arrest, protest, dispute or complaint is recorded, compensation is recorded as fully paid at the rates in the resettlement plan, and the follow-up study of 264 households and the borrower's survey of 217 directly affected households both report living standards restored or improved. The works were 17 rehabilitation segments of 840.845 km and 7 improvement segments of 320.6 km scattered across a province, with no named village, neighbourhood or community in either document. ICIJ puts displacement at 14,821; no figure of 14,821 appears in the documents and they do not explain the gap. At appraisal the survey had put house relocation at 31,194 square metres affecting 680 people in 175 households. A redacted Integrity Vice Presidency investigation report for this project was disclosed on 13 January 2012, but it is a fiduciary matter and neither the completion report nor the Group's review ties it to the resettlement.

dropped.candidate: China Bengbu Integrated Environment Improvement Project (P096925)
dropped.reason: No World Bank document counts the people or households relocated. The completion report of 7 March 2016 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 17 March 2017 were both read in full. They record 60 hectares permanently acquired against about 182 planned, 35,572 square metres of housing demolished against 103,160 planned, and 5,824 project affected people at closing against 11,128 at appraisal - all of them counts of people affected, not relocated. The one household count is the 273 households, 1,094 people, affected by two roads added at restructuring, again as affected. The nearest thing to a relocation count is the 40 displaced households in Huaiyuan County who had not moved into their resettlement housing when the loan closed in June 2015; the documents say they had chosen that site over a completed one a kilometre away, had signed agreements, had received their compensation and 30 months of transitional housing rent, and were expected to move by June 2017 under continued external monitoring. The 40 households are the nearest thing in the file to a count of households displaced, and they fail the second limb of the rule: the documents record that each had signed an agreement for a named apartment by the end of May 2015, had received all other compensation, and was paid 30 months of transitional housing rent into a bank account by the county government, to be doubled if the transitional period ran longer, and that they had chosen to wait for the Jiankang Huayuan site because it was closer to the central urban area with better infrastructure and transport. The documents record no death, injury, arrest, protest or unpaid compensation anywhere in the project, and say compensation standards were raised to replacement cost at the time of implementation rather than the rates set in the resettlement plan about two years earlier. So the project records no count of anyone relocated and no failure, and it is a drop rather than a case. ICIJ puts displacement at 11,521, which is close to but not the same as the appraisal figure of 11,128 affected people. The project area is also the Bengbu reach of the Huai River, where the map already carries `huai-river-flood-drainage-resettlement` at 32.9156, 117.3892, so a case here would have needed checking against that one as well.
